source: Forbus, Gentner, Law (1994) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19
finding: Two-stage retrieval. MAC is a cheap pass: each description gets a count vector of predicate (functor) types, and memory items are ranked by dot product with the probe vector. FAC then runs the full structural matcher (SME) only on the MAC survivors and keeps the best match plus any within a set margin.
numbers: Both stages use a selector that keeps the best score plus all items within 10% of it. Dot product cost about 0.002 s per vector pair in their Lisp setup. MAC/FAC was about two orders of magnitude faster than ARCS on the same data.
limits: 1994 symbolic predicate-calculus inputs written by hand. Needs structured representations; text must first be parsed.
agent_relevance: A usable recipe for memory retrieval in O7: cheap type-count filter over stored problem records, then structural scoring on a short list only.

source: Forbus, Gentner, Law (1994) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19 (human target data, Karla the Hawk stories)
finding: The human data MAC/FAC is fitted to: people are reminded of surface-similar stories far more often than analogous ones, even though they rate analogous matches as more sound.
numbers: 32 stories studied, 20 probes (5 each of LS, AN, SF, FOR). Proportion of remindings: SF .53, AN .12, FOR .03 (LS value is unreadable in the scan). Order LS >= SF > AN >= FOR, stable over three variations. Gick and Holyoak figure cited: about 30% solve the radiation problem unprompted vs 80-90% when told to use the story.
limits: Numbers are quoted in the 1994 paper from Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus 1993 and Rattermann and Gentner 1987; those primaries were not opened. Scan OCR dropped the LS cell.
agent_relevance: Retrieval by an unaided reasoner is surface-driven. Our agent should not expect far analogues to surface without an explicit structural query.

source: Forbus, Gentner, Law (1994) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19 simulation 1
finding: MAC/FAC reproduces the human order LS > SF > AN with the base story in memory among FOR distractors, but does much better than people overall.
numbers: Memory 18 stories (9 base, 9 FOR); probes 27 (9 each LS, SF, AN). Correct base retrieved through MAC and FAC: LS 1.0, SF 0.89, AN 0.67.
limits: Memory far smaller than the 32 stories plus background knowledge of people, and no one-week delay.
agent_relevance: Even a cheap vector filter finds about two thirds of true analogues when the pool is small. Pool size is the thing to watch.

source: Forbus, Gentner, Law (1994) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19 simulations 2 and 3
finding: With harder memories MAC/FAC still matches the human order. FAC acts as a structural filter on what MAC passes. With no literal matches in memory, surface matches win.
numbers: Sim 2: memory 36 stories (9 sets x LS,SF,AN,FOR); LS .78 through both stages; other cells garbled in scan. Mean items passed by MAC 3.4, accepted by FAC 1.6. Sim 3 (27 stories, no LS): FAC returned SF .78, AN .56, FOR .11, other .11; MAC passed SF .88, AN .56, FOR .22, other 1.11.
limits: Table cells partly garbled by OCR; ordering and the 3.4 / 1.6 means are clean.
agent_relevance: A structural second stage cuts junk (other-set hits 1.11 down to .11). Keep a verify step after cheap retrieval.

source: Forbus, Gentner, Law (1994) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19 sensitivity analysis one (selector width)
finding: MAC/FAC fits the human data only in a middle band of filter widths. Too narrow never retrieves analogies. Too wide gives too many analogies, then junk.
numbers: Viable region: MAC width 10-20% with FAC at least 10%. MAC 1% or FAC 1%: analogies never retrieved. MAC 30% or more with wide FAC: junk remindings. Binary content vectors: viable MAC band shifted to 30-50%; mean output size 2 vs 1.5.
limits: Fitted to one story set family (Karla, 9 sets).
agent_relevance: Shortlist size is a real tuning knob: keep 1-3 candidates, not top-20.

source: Forbus, Gentner, Law (1994) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19 sensitivity analyses two and three (what goes in the vector)
finding: Content vector normalisation hardly matters. What matters is mixing attribute and relation information: vectors built from attributes only, or from relations only, fail to reproduce the human pattern.
numbers: Attribute-only vectors: no viable region at all. Relation-only vectors: also fail (junk when MAC at 40% or FAC above 70%; viable only in a narrow MAC band).
limits: Authors say further tests are needed with other domains.
agent_relevance: A pure structure-only filter is not better. Keep a few surface cues in the cheap stage so near matches are not lost.

source: Forbus, Gentner, Law (1994) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19 section 6 comparison with ARCS (Thagard et al. 1990)
finding: The rival connectionist retrieval model ARCS gets the human order wrong and is swamped by larger memories. MAC/FAC is stable and far faster.
numbers: ARCS asymptotic activations for Karla probes: LS .67, FOR -.11, SF -.17, AN -.27 (so SF and AN below FOR). Adding 25 plays to 100 fables left MAC/FAC unchanged but made ARCS retrieve plays for a fable probe. ARCS runtimes 81-5133 s vs MAC/FAC 0.2-26 s. Authors could not get ARCS to settle on many of their encodings (runs up to 12 h).
limits: Self-comparison by MAC/FAC authors; ARCS retrieval criterion was undefined and they copied Thagard cutoffs.
agent_relevance: Supports the simple two-stage design over heavy constraint networks.

source: Forbus, Gentner, Law (1994) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19 Hamlet and West Side Story probes
finding: On Shakespeare plays, MAC/FAC retrieved Romeo and Juliet for West Side Story with a strong structural score, but for Hamlet the structural stage was indifferent.
numbers: West Side Story: FAC score 16.51 for Romeo and Juliet (near isomorphic). Hamlet: FAC 6.79 R&J, 5.49 Julius Caesar, 3.72 Macbeth, 2.67 Othello; the drop to the next item is 20%. MAC top for Hamlet was Othello .86, Macbeth .85, R&J .83.
limits: Hand-encoded plays from the ARCS data set; two probes only.
agent_relevance: Structural scores are lumpy: near-isomorphic matches stand out sharply, loose ones do not. A threshold on the structural score can say no good analogue honestly.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nature Human Behaviour (arXiv 2212.09196)
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) given Gentner-style story pairs chose the target that shared causal relations with the source, but unlike people it did not do so reliably in the far (cross-domain) condition.
numbers: Humans N=54 UCLA students; 15 of 54 picked the analogous story on every trial. Combined binomial p=.0005 for GPT-3. Near: GPT-3 p=.0039. Far: GPT-3 not significant. Humans beat GPT-3 on this task (OR 0.37, p=.0003). First GPT-4 look: near perfect near, stronger far.
limits: Forced choice between two given stories, not retrieval from memory. GPT-3 generation, early.
agent_relevance: Recognising a far analogue when shown it is not the same as finding it. Both gaps shrink with model scale.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer, Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives, TACL
finding: Models pick near analogies well and far analogies badly. Embedding similarity (SBERT) is surface-bound: good on near, about 1% on far.
numbers: Zero-shot: near analogies models avg 75.0% vs humans 97.9% (random 50%). Far analogies models avg 39.6% (below random) vs humans 94.1%. GPT-4 avg 68.1%, SBERT avg 42.3%, GPT-4 below random on far. Overall human 96% vs models 57%. Best far-analogy/near-distractor setting went to UnifiedQA-11B.
quote: even the largest ones struggle with far analogies in a zero-shot setting, with GPT4.0 scoring below random
limits: Binary choice task built from ePiC proverb narratives; one analogue vs one distractor.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that off-the-shelf similarity (embeddings) fails where MAC/FAC's second stage is meant to help: far analogues with a near-surface decoy.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN, demonstration and chain-of-thought experiments
finding: Plain solved examples barely helped and hurt on near analogies. Examples with a step to state each narrative's high-level message first helped far analogies a lot.
numbers: CoT demonstrations (2, 4 or 6, half far, half near): GPT models gained up to 30 absolute points on far analogies vs zero-shot. Near analogies stayed below zero-shot with CoT. Far-analogy demos were slightly more helpful than near ones. Telling models to find system mappings vs just similarity made only a small difference.
limits: Run on Llama-2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4; exact per-cell numbers only in figures.
agent_relevance: A scaffold step that first abstracts each case to its gist (a proverb-like message) before comparing is a cheap analogue of structural indexing. Gains up to 30 points.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: Deriving story-level analogies from LLMs, EMNLP
finding: Sentence-embedding similarity is a poor indicator of story analogy. It works for literal similarity retrieval. LLMs pick surface-similar hard negatives about as often as the true analogue.
numbers: Multiple choice (4 options, random 25%): humans 85.7%, text-davinci-003 averages 37.1%. Prior analogy retrieval model of Sultan and Shahaf: 44.9%. Models chose easy negatives under 20% of the time (chance 50%) but often chose the nounal-similarity hard negative as much as the target. Fine-tuned RoBERTa variants gave the best analogy-score correlation.
limits: Benchmark stories are partly GPT-generated; annotation Fleiss kappa 47% (entity) and 42% (relation).
agent_relevance: Confirms surface-first retrieval in modern models. A structure-aware retriever (a 2022 clustering one) beat vanilla LLM choice.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy, generation and prevalence
finding: Analogies are rare in ordinary text, so they are hard to find by search. Few-shot demos from the corpus raise analogy generation quality.
numbers: Analogies about 3% of a scientific corpus (cited from Sultan and Shahaf 2023). Few demos lifted LLaMa generation quality by +28.4 and +27.5 points on two measures; ChatGPT improved moderately. 40 test source stories.
limits: The 3% figure is second-hand (cited, not opened).
agent_relevance: Base rate is low: a retrieval step that fires on every problem will mostly return nothing useful. Gate it, as the schema already does at impasses.

source: Ye, Wang, Choi, Lu, Sharma, Shen, Tiyyala, Andrews, Khashabi (2024) AnaloBench: Benchmarking the identification of abstract and long-context analogies, EMNLP
finding: T1 (pick the analogy among 4): every model is below humans, and accuracy falls as the story gets longer, while humans plateau. Scale helps on one-sentence stories but plateaus on 10- and 30-sentence stories.
numbers: 340 human-written analogies, 12 open and 3 proprietary models. Random 25%. No model beat humans at any story length (1, 10, 30 sentences). Human annotators unanimous on 47 of 50 one-sentence analogies.
quote: scale offers minimal gains when, (i) analogies involve lengthy scenarios, or (ii) recalling relevant scenarios from a large pool
limits: GPT-4 also wrote the 10 and 30 sentence expansions; a Claude-generated check showed GPT-4 still did better, so self-preference is unlikely to explain it.
agent_relevance: Long case records make analogical judging harder. Store short abstracts of past cases, not full transcripts.

source: Ye et al. (2024) AnaloBench, task T2 (retrieve analogies from a 200-story bank)
finding: Asked to list the top 10 analogous stories from a bank of 200, GPT-4-turbo and Claude-v2 are near random except for one-sentence stories with GPT-4-turbo.
numbers: GPT-4-turbo 1-sentence: P@3 42.9%, P@5 38.5%, MAP 55.4%, MRR 64.2%. 10-sentence: P@3 6.5%, MAP 14.2%, MRR 15.6%. 30-sentence: P@3 3.9%, MAP 10.8%, MRR 11.3%. Claude-v2 1-sentence P@3 10.2%, MRR 18.9%. Random P@3 3.9%, MAP 1.7%, MRR 11.1%. Oracle R@5 81.6%.
limits: No human score for T2 (too costly). Only long-context models run. Models read the whole bank in context rather than using an index. Row labels in the appendix table are partly scrambled; the first block is read as GPT-4-turbo.
agent_relevance: Letting the model scan a pool for analogues itself does not work at length. External structured retrieval (MAC/FAC-like) has a real job to do.

source: Su et al. (2025) BRIGHT: A realistic and challenging benchmark for reasoning-intensive retrieval, ICLR
finding: When relevance needs reasoning (same theorem, same logic, not the same words) the best embedding models score very low.
numbers: 1,384 queries, 12 datasets. SFR-EmbeddingMistral: MTEB retrieval 59.0 but BRIGHT nDCG@10 18.3 (abstract). Best average in the main table 24.3. BM25 14.5 average. 13 retrievers tested.
limits: Not an analogy benchmark as such; includes theorem and similar-problem retrieval, which is the closest to structural reuse.
agent_relevance: Standard dense retrieval is weak when the match is by method, not topic. Do not rely on an off-the-shelf embedding for O7 retrieval.

source: Su et al. (2025) BRIGHT, query rewriting with reasoning
finding: Having an LLM first write a step-by-step reasoning trace about the query and using that as the search query raises scores sharply. BM25 on GPT-4 reasoning becomes best on the leaderboard.
numbers: Average gain up to 12.2 nDCG@10 points. Prompt: identify the essential problem, reason about what relevant documents contain, draft an answer. GPT-4 and Llama-3-70B reasoning helped clearly; GritLM-written reasoning helped less.
limits: Extra LLM call per query. Rewriting may import the LLM's own errors.
agent_relevance: Cheap, scaffold-only version of retrieve-by-structure: describe the problem's abstract structure in words, then search with that description.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, ICLR
finding: Instead of retrieving past problems, ask the model to recall relevant problems itself and then solve. It beat 0-shot CoT and manual few-shot CoT.
numbers: GSM8K: 5-shot CoT 75.0% (GPT-3.5-turbo), self-generated exemplars 75.8-77.8% by variant; text-davinci-003 14.8% to 50.3-61.0%; PaLM2 60.8% to 78.2-81.7%. MATH: GPT-3.5-turbo 33.0% to 33.9-37.3%; PaLM2 27.1% to 29.8-34.8%. Average gain about +4% over baselines.
limits: Variant rows differ by exemplar count and whether knowledge is added; exact row labels were lost in text extraction.
agent_relevance: The self-recall prompt is a zero-infrastructure form of analogical retrieval. Good fallback when no memory store exists.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024), generated versus retrieved exemplars
finding: Self-generated exemplars beat retrieved exemplars on stronger models. Retrieval from a labelled set wins on weak models.
numbers: GSM8K: curie-001 retrieved CoT better; davinci-002 retrieved 47% vs self-generated 48%; davinci-003 retrieved 54% vs self-generated 57-61%. Retrieval by cosine similarity, top K=5. Codeforces: GPT-3.5-turbo with generated knowledge plus exemplars Acc@1 15% vs GPT-4 16%.
limits: Retrieval was plain cosine similarity, not structure-aware. Table 4 row alignment is approximate in the text extraction.
agent_relevance: Model strength decides the route: a strong model can invent its own analogues; a weak one needs a verified store.

source: Rubin, Herzig, Berant (2022) Learning to retrieve prompts for in-context learning, NAACL (arXiv 2112.08633)
finding: A retriever trained on which examples actually help the language model beats similarity retrieval (BM25, SBERT, CBR). Task-useful is not the same as surface-similar.
numbers: Exact match: BREAK BM25 26.0, CBR 25.7, EPR 31.9 (LM-oracle 43.1). MTOP BM25 52.9, CBR 57.0, EPR 64.2. SMCalFlow BM25 46.1, CBR 51.4, EPR 54.3. Random: 1.7, 7.3, 8.9.
limits: Needs a training set with labels and a scoring LM; semantic parsing, not open reasoning.
agent_relevance: Retrieval quality should be judged by downstream gain, not by similarity score. Our agent can log which retrieved items helped and reweight.

source: Levy, Bogin, Berant (2023) Diverse demonstrations improve in-context compositional generalization, ACL
finding: Choosing demonstrations by similarity alone gives repetitive prompts that miss needed structures. Choosing a set that covers the target program's local structures helps a lot.
numbers: Up to +23 absolute points over similarity retrieval (SMCalFlow-CS 50.3 to 73.5). Oracle top-K similarity was beaten by oracle structure coverage in 7 of 8 compositional splits. Cover-LS beat DPP diversity in 7 of 10 splits. Prompts of 24 demonstrations.
limits: Semantic parsing with known output grammar; coverage needs predicted structures. Random did well on small synthetic COVR-10.
agent_relevance: Retrieve a set that jointly covers the sub-structures a problem needs, not the k nearest neighbours. Maps to picking 2 complementary analogues.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners, AAAI (arXiv 2308.10144)
finding: An agent that stores successful trajectories and retrieves them by task similarity beats random selection, and retrieval and extracted insights are complementary.
numbers: ALFWorld success: ReAct 40.0%, random successful trajectories 42.5%, reason-similarity retrieval 48.5%, task-similarity retrieval (ExpeL) 59.0%. Retrieval-only vs insights-only: ALFWorld 55% vs 50%; HotpotQA 31% vs 36%.
limits: Retrieval is by task-description embedding (FAISS), not structure. Textual environments only.
agent_relevance: Working in-loop example of memory retrieval with an ablation: similar-task retrieval is worth about 16 points over random on ALFWorld.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Thought Propagation: An analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs, ICLR (arXiv 2310.03965)
finding: The model proposes analogous problems, solves them, and aggregates their solutions to refine the answer. No external memory; analogues are generated, not retrieved.
numbers: Tasks: 100 shortest-path problems, creative writing, LLM-agent planning (ALFWorld). TP beat IO, CoT and ToT on optimal-path rate across PaLM-2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4. ToT underperformed plain IO on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 and failed on PaLM-2. Two layers gave marginal gain over one at more token cost. In planning TP gained without any failure-memory module.
limits: Exact table cells not extracted here. Analogy quality depends on model-written problems.
agent_relevance: A one-layer propose-solve-aggregate loop is affordable and fits O7. Do not stack layers.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: Thought-augmented reasoning with LLMs, NeurIPS (arXiv 2406.04271)
finding: A meta-buffer of distilled thought templates is retrieved by embedding similarity between a distilled problem and template descriptions; the template is instantiated for the task. Buffer is updated only when no good template matched.
numbers: Versus Meta-prompting: +23% Game of 24, +20% Geometric Shapes, +51% Checkmate-in-One. GPT-4 baseline to BoT on Game of 24: +79.4% accuracy; +8.4% over ToT. Success rate over 10 repeated runs on 1000 samples: about +10% over second best.
limits: Retrieval is plain embedding similarity over abstracted descriptions. Task families are narrow and repetitive. Ablation numbers are in figures only.
agent_relevance: Closest published thing to indexing by abstract structure: retrieve a template by a distilled description, not raw text.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2402.08955)
finding: A partial failed replication of Webb et al.: GPT models do worse than humans on letter-string analogies even in the normal alphabet, and fall sharply with permuted or symbol alphabets. Humans stay flat.
numbers: Overall accuracy: humans .753 (1,876 samples, 136 Prolific participants), GPT-3 .488, GPT-3.5 .350, GPT-4 .452. Error types differ: GPT-4 incorrect-rule 32.7%, humans 14.7% (column assignment from the error table, approximate).
limits: Letter strings, not retrieval. Different prompt format from Webb may explain part of the gap.
agent_relevance: Analogical skill in models may lean on seen patterns. Retrieval of an analogue is only as good as the model's ability to re-map it to new content.

source: Stevenson, Pafford, van der Maas, Mitchell (2025) Can large language models generalize analogy solving like children can? (arXiv 2411.02348)
finding: Children (7-9) and adults transfer letter-string analogy rules to an unfamiliar alphabet; four recent LLMs do not.
numbers: 42 children, 62 adults, 55 runs each of Claude-3.5, Gemma-2 27B, GPT-4o, Llama-3.1 405B. Zero-shot, Latin, Greek (near) and symbol (far) alphabets. For each model performance degraded in the unfamiliar alphabets; humans stayed similar. All models sometimes used a literal copy rule that humans never used.
limits: Letter-string domain only. The methods text gives 68 adults and 44 children, the introduction 62 and 42; the introduction figures are used.
agent_relevance: Transfer across surface forms is the weak spot, which is what far-analogue reuse needs.

source: Yuan, Chen, Ge, Xiao, Yang (2023) Beneath surface similarity: LLMs make reasonable scientific analogies after structure abduction (arXiv 2305.12660)
finding: High word-analogy scores do not show structure mapping. Models that do well on a relational structure test often fail the word analogy test, so the two measure different things.
numbers: SCAR benchmark: 400 scientific system analogies, 632 systems, 1,614 concept mappings, 13 fields. GPT-4 best but below humans (2 graduate students). GPT-4 at human level on most word-analogy sets but well behind on E-KAR.
limits: Human baseline is only two people. Exact accuracy cells not extracted.
agent_relevance: Do not trust word-level analogy benchmarks as evidence the model can do structural retrieval.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-based reasoning for retrieval augmented generation in LLMs for legal question answering (arXiv 2404.04302)
finding: Case retrieval by fine-tuned embeddings added to a generator gave only a small gain. A hybrid of question and support-text embeddings did best. This is case-based retrieval, not structure mapping.
numbers: Best hybrid AnglEBERT with 3 neighbours: +1.94% semantic similarity over no-RAG, significant at 95% (one-tailed t-test) vs No-RAG and hybrid LegalBERT; 90% vs hybrid BERT k=1. Full cases in the prompt beat support text alone. 32 test cases only; Mistral-7B generator.
limits: Tiny test set; metric is embedding cosine to a reference answer, not correctness.
agent_relevance: Cautionary: embedding case retrieval gives small gains when the model already holds the knowledge.

source: Sultan and Shahaf (2023) Life is a circus and we are the clowns: automatically finding analogies between situations and processes
finding: Cited in StoryAnalogy: an analogy-mining system using entity clustering and mapping between clusters; resists surface decoys better than LLMs.
numbers: Scored 44.9% on StoryAnalogy multiple choice (random 25%). Analogies found in about 3% of a scientific corpus (as cited).
limits: Not opened; numbers come from the StoryAnalogy paper. Original not read.
agent_relevance: A pre-LLM structure-aware miner outperformed GPT-3.5-era LLMs on surface-decoy items.
